title: What To Say To A Needy, Dependent Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the surge of neediness common at the start of a school year, explaining it as a symptom of learned helplessness from prior teachers who over-helped. Even after clear instruction and modeling, some students freeze and silently plead for assistance. He offers five specific lines teachers can say — while maintaining physical distance and withholding sympathy — to push students back toward independence, such as 'You don't need me' and 'What is your plan?' He acknowledges the approach may feel harsh but argues it is the more compassionate long-term choice, since it dismantles false praise-driven dependence and lets students build a real, earned sense of competence.
points: Identifies learned helplessness, often instilled by previous over-helping teachers, as the root of first-month neediness.
Offers five exact phrases to use with needy students, including 'You don't need me,' 'I believe in you,' and 'So what is your plan?'
Instructs teachers to keep physical distance and withhold visible sympathy when responding to pleas for help.
Warns that initial struggle and lower output are expected and even beneficial, since they reveal students' true baseline ability.
Argues the goal is to let students experience real, unaided success so that subsequent praise is genuinely earned and motivating.
quotes: Just be sure you keep some physical distance between you and them. Do not lean down, kneel next to them, or show any sympathy.
1. “You don’t need me.” 2. “You can do this.” 3. “I believe in you.
At first, yes. There is a chance they won’t get much done. But this is okay. It’s even good, because it’s really them.
Being forced, essentially, to either sit and do nothing or succeed, which you’ve prepared them for, is a powerful motivator to pursue the latter.
It cranks their intrinsic motivational engine on for the first time, turning their world upside down.
